It would appear to me to be a very reasonable request to ask the United States government to enter upon a discussion of this question. The hon. member for Welland made it perfectly clear that that was all he was asking for; he was not asking the government to bind itself. He pointed out the fact that the United States government had about a year ago made to the Canadian government a proposition to discuss this question, but the Canadian government then thought the time was not opportune for such a discussion.
Before I say a few more words regarding that, I wish to deal with a few of the statements made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar). I will deal with them very briefly. In his closing remarks he seemed to draw the conclusion that the whole idea of the building of the St. Lawrence-Great Lakes canal was the outcome of some imaginative chap at Fort William; that Fort William, being anxious to be an ocean port, had come forward with this proposition and decided to belabour the rest of the country into building the St. Lawrence-Great Lakes canal. That, at least, was the conclusion I drew from his remarks. As a matter of fact, the original pro-
Supply-Canals

position, so far as I remember-and I think I am correct-started in the north-western states of the Union amongst the grain growers, and the organization gradually became strong and large until the movement took hold of the Canadian people, and the first meeting was held at Windsor, the home of the late Minister of Railways.
I certainly had no thought whatever that the idea had started at Fort William. I do not know what I said to give my hon. friend that impression.
The hon. member said that he did not know why the Welland canal was being built, but that Fort William seemed to be anxious to be an ocean port.
Among others.

He did not say "among others"; he is saying that now. However, that does not matter. I wish to supplement what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) stated regarding ocean steamers. I believe that no one who has studied the question expects ocean steamers to any great extent ever to go to the Great Lakes even to Toronto or Windsor, or to the head of the lakes or Duluth. It is anticipated that if the canal system is ever built, as I have no doubt at all it ultimately will be, those ships taking grain from the head of the lakes and Duluth will be able to carry it to Montreal at a much less cost than is charged at the present time, and without transshipping at Port Colborne or the Georgian bay ports or at Buffalo and going down by the Erie canal to New York. There is not a thought, on the part of those who have given any study to the question, of great ocean steamers landing at the docks at the head of the lakes.
In regard to the building of the Welland canal, I have the same to say as I have said concerning the St. Lawrence system: certainly, Fort William has had no idea of asking for any particular consideration in this respect. There was no move on the part of the people at the head of the lakes in this matter. Naturally, Fort William and the head of the lakes are directly interested in the building of the canal and are supporting it in consequence; but they do so with the complete conviction that it is a good thing in the interests of the country. My hon. friend spoke about rates on grain and pointed out, what he has already indicated to me in private, namely the rates for which grain was carried from the head of the lakes to Montreal previous to the war; and I must confess that when he showed me the figures I was startled by the low charge that was made upon grain I Mr. Manion.]
over that distance. At the same time, we must not forget that twenty or fifteen years ago everything was very much lower than it is to-day, and I greatly doubt whether we shall ever get back to such rates as the hon. gentleman quoted, such as an average of 4 cents for grain from the head of the lakes to Montreal. Later on in his remarks he pointed out-at least I understood him to do so-that a water rate from the head of the lakes to Montreal of 11 cents was a reasonable one. I think I am quoting the hon. gentleman correctly in that regard. Well, I would consider that a very unreasonable rate if we had the St. Lawrence waterway built.
Would that be 11 cents a bushel?

Yes. I should think that if the large shell-like boats at the head of the lakes can transport grain clear through to Montreal, then certainly the rate ought ultimately, except under very special circumstances, to be nothing like 11 cents.
It should be more like 3 cents.

Yes; probably 3 or 4 cents would cover it, and my hon. friend would then get back to the rates which he quoted as prevailing before the war. The hon. gentleman made the statement, which is correct, that some time ago about 65 per cent of the grain grown in western Canada was shipped to the United Kingdom via New York, in this way: It would come from the head of the lakes to Buffalo, and thence by the Erie canal to New York. The charge from Buffalo to New York alone was 10 cents; and yet my hon. friend points out- what is the fact-that the shippers generally, at least two-thirds of them, chose the American route. They did this for various reasons, and in spite of the fact that they had to pay 10 cents for the carriage from Buffalo by the Erie canal to New York city alone. That is another reason, and an important one, why. if the canal is ultimately built, grain will be carried at a much lower rate than is the case at the present time. I believe my hon. friend stated that in the past year a large proportion of Canadian grain went via New York.
I do not think that last year such a large proportion did go by New York; I believe that at least two-thirds went via Montreal.

There went by Montreal
153,000,000 bushels.

Well, 153,000,000 is a very large proportion of our grain. That is what I understood-about 150,000,000

Yes; my hon. friend, I think, is correct in that regard. However, that is beside the question. Now, I might observe here that one of the greatest authorities on the grain question in the world, as my hon. friends to my left will no doubt agree, is Julius Barnes. He is at all events one of the most reliable authorities, and he has made the statement again and again that the carrying out of this undertaking would save from five to ten cents a bushel on wheat being shipped to Europe. And Herbert Hoover, a man who is internationally known, has also expressed the same view. If we look at the report of the International Joint Commission we shall also find exactly the same thing stated. After two years of study, after a very thorough investigation, they come to precisely the same conclusion, that a great saving would be made to the western farmer by building the canal. In view of these facts, and in view of the statements mads by Julius Barnes, by Herbert Hoover and by this commission, I certainly think that the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) makes a quite reasonable request when he asks the government to extend an invitation to the American government to discuss this question from the standpoint of the feasibility of the project. I would repeat and support what he said. Such a request would not bind the Canadian government to anything, and I certainly believe that the discussion would lead to practical results. It would undoubtedly be a thorough one, and before either government undertook to commit itself, it would no
doubt be convinced that the scheme was in the best interests of both countries.
I believe, from the report of the commission, and in view of the fact that we shall have spent $100,000,000 on the Welland canal, that the St. Lawrence-Great Lakes canal could be built for a very small sum of money so far as Canada's share is concerned. And if in raising the money the two governments united in guaranteeing bonds at 4 per cent or 4^ per cent, the necessary funds I have no doubt could be obtained. If the respective governments united in the undertaking, it would not necessarily entail the expenditure of one cent directly by the government of this country. I submit once more that the request that the government take steps to bring about a discussion of this question between representatives of the Canadian administration and of the United States government is undoubtedly a reasonable one, and I hope that in the near future the government now in power will extend an invitation to this end to the neighbouring republic and take up the matter.

My hon. friend from Qu'-Appelle (Mr. Millar) criticizes the cost of the Welland canal, now estimated at not less than $80,000,000 and perhaps more, and he points out that the original estimate was some $55,000,000. This seems to him to be proof that the estimates are now too high. But I would point out that these were pre-war estimates and the contracts of necessity had to be dropped on account of the war. Had there been no war the estimated cost, I imagine, would not have been exceeded to any great extent. But to-day everything costs twice as much as it did before the war, and I think I am safe in saying that an expenditure of ninety million dollars now is no more extravagant than fifty-five million dollars would have been at pre-war prices. So there is nothing strange or wrong about the increased expenditure.
Now, my hon. friend refers to the Oswego canal. I would suggest that he need not worry any more about that. Those who were opposed to the deepening of the Welland canal years ago-I refer now to Buffalo interests largely-always tried to frighten us with the bugaboo of what they were going to do to us on the Erie canal by way of Oswego. As a matter of fact a large appropriation was secured from the state of New York for the canal. I have read of the hopes they had of a 20 or 25-foot draft channel. But the best engineers reported that 12 feet was the best draft they could get, and that not in all places. But in addition to that there are

hundreds of bridges over the Erie canal of only 15 feet clearance, and these would have to be raised. With a straight route now from the Welland canal through to-I must say both Kingston or Prescott, or perhaps as a compromise, Brockville-sufficient for vessels drawing 21 feet, my hon. friend can see the absolute impossibility of the Erie canal with its little 12-foot draft and its 15-foot overhead bridge clearance competing with such a route. Even we are complaining that the draft is small and we have to use barges, but our shallowest draft is two feet deeper than the Erie canal's maximum. So at the very best we can carry through our canal, even as at present constituted, much heavier loads than the Erie canal can ever accommodate.

I think the minister has
overlooked one statement I made, that at the present time all but 14 per cent of the grain reaching New York comes by rail; that is, the Erie canal is not cutting very much of a figure in the competition now.

That is true, and it never will. But Buffalo, so far as the Oswego route is concerned, could compete via New York by rail and not use the canal at all. The object of the Welland canal deepening is to bring the traffic of the West as far east as possible before transshipping it into smaller boats. Sir William Van Horne on one occasion when discussing this very project stated that he believed it was as cheap to transship to shallower draft vessels at the foot of lake Ontario or farther east and take the cargoes to Montreal as it would be to have larger vessels for the whole route, but I am not going to discuss that subject at the present time. However if the Welland canal deepening will not decrease the cost of transportation of western grain, it will not do anything. I think it will. Some few years ago I had an opportunity of discussing the figures with those engaged in transportation, and, although those figures would not be applicable now,
I was informed by these people that they believed there would be an appreciable reduction in the cost of transportation of grain and other products eastward as far as Kingston and Prescott. My hon. friend refers to a saving of one cent a bushel. Does he realize that such a saving or even half of it, on Canada's grain crop would mean a saving of millions of dollars?
When I was speaking the other night I was mildly castigated for suggesting that the western people ever asked for the deepening of the Welland canal. Of course, a great many of the members from the West now are young men, and they perhaps do not re-

member what happened years ago, but I made several trips through to the coast with Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1907 and 1910-shortly before the calamity befell this country-and one of the main things dwelt upon at every meeting in the West was:	When are you
going to start deepening the Welland canal? Deputations from one part of the West were urging the construction of the Hudson Bay railway, but from the time we struck Winnipeg until we reached Victoria the Welland canal deepening was mentioned by nearly every deputation that came to us. I asked my secretary to see if anything could be found in the way of representations from boards of trade and other associations that were sent to the department, because hundreds of representations were made orally to every minister of the then government who went West. At random I find the following representations were received: From AVinni-peg, Vancouver, Edmonton, Port Arthur, Kamloops, Virden, Victoria, Camrose, Regina, the Winnipeg Grain and Produce Exchange, the Selkirk Business Men's Association, and so forth. I dare say if I were to go to Brockville and open up several boxes of correspondence marked "private" I could dig up hundreds of these representations from the AVest. But the deepening of the canal is started, and it is for the purpose of making transportation cheaper in the Dominion both east and west. AA'e believe it will accomplish that object. It has cost more money than was anticipated. So has everything else in this country. Even a meal costs more to-day than it did in 1913. One of the difficulties of carrying on national affairs to-day is that everything is much more expensive than it was a few years ago.

Some time ago the Canadian government did receive a communication from the United States government suggesting a conference with a view to making a treaty, but the Canadian government at that time did not see its way clear to proceeding so rapidly in the matter. At a later date a large deputation

waited on the Prime Minister and others, when the Prime Minister suggested if I remember correctly, that he would gladly consider it if the United States would make another proposition for a conference without going so far as to say that it was for the purpose of making a treaty. I think my hon. friend was mistaken in saying that the United States government offered to pay a substantial part of the construction cost of the Welland canal.
That was recommended by the International Joint Commission.

That recommendation was made by the International Joint Commission in a report containing certain references to each government. Of course, the matter of a great St. Lawrence waterway is very interesting to me. Having lived on the St. Lawrence most of my life perhaps I take a deeper interest in the matter than others not so situated. It is a very big problem and without consulting the other members of the government I would not like to say anything definite as to holding another conference between the United States government and the Dominion of Canada. There are other interests concerned in the proposition besides the Dominion of Canada and the United States. The federal authority, of course, takes cognizance of improvements to navigation, but the construction of the proposed St. Lawrence deep waterway would mean the development of a very substantial amount of power. I am free to admit that this part of Ontario at least is in need of power. In some sections we have the Hydro Electric power, but in most cases it has to be transmitted over such a distance that it is really not cheap power, particularly in places where the consumption does not extend to any great degree. The provincial authorities have also something to say in the water itself, and as hon. gentlemen will remember there have been some disagreements as to the legal rights as between the federal and the provincial authorities. However, I think it has been pretty clearly demonstrated that so far as the water itself is concerned the provincial authorities have at least some ground for making their claim. Then, of course, there is the state authority on the other side of the line. When last I mentioned this in the House some years ago I added another factor, the International Joint Commission, but the commission has since made certain propositions to each government particularly as to the Welland canal. The Welland canal construction was' started years ago before the suggestion for the St. Lawrence deep waterway had taken definite shape, I
imagine. But this one thing is assured, that the deepening of the Welland canal will form the beginning of that enterprise so far as the connection between the two lakes is concerned, and if the time comes for the proposal of the International Joint Commission to be put into effect Canada will be in a position to lay claim to the share which the United States ought to pay for the construction of the Welland canal.

I would like to say a word or two on this subject inasmuch as I come from a city that is spending twenty-six millions in rebuilding the port of Toronto and improving and enlarging its harbour anticipating that a contract had been made between the cities and towns on the St. Lawrence and on lakes Erie and Ontario and the upper lakes with the government regarding the deepening of this canal. A study of the canal situation in Canada does not disclose any definite and consistent plan such as the people of Canada had in 1829 when the Welland canal was first started. It is true also that water-borne traffic has not had the chance it should have had in competition with the railways of this country, and for that reason we have congestion every year not only in handling the wheat crop but coal and every other basic commodity in this country. Water-borne traffic got no subsidies, bonuses, land grants or hand-outs like railways did.
Money has been spent on some canals that never should have been constructed in the first place and left unspent on others, and three transcontinental railways have been built where probably one or two would have sufficed. The people of this country have spent $900,000,000 directly and indirectly upon the railways of this country, and still we have congestion half the time and the deplorable situation in which the railways are to-day. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, the canals have never had the chance they should have had, and if some of the money that has been spent on any one of these transcontinental railways had been spent on deepening the St. Lawrence waterway and the Welland canal, and in addition if money had not been spent on canals that can have no economic value, we would have had much better value for our money and should have taken a great step forward in solving the transportation problems of this country.
As shown by this deep waterways report the Welland canal is one of the most important links in the whole St. Lawrence waterway scheme. The history of the Welland canal goes back to 1829 when the government

Supply-Canals

of Canada, assisted by the British government built the first canal. It was supposed to be a four foot canal, but its dimensions were subsequently changed to the following: a 40 foot lock, 110 feet long, 20 feet wide, with 8 feet of water over the sills. On the union of Upper and Lower Canada in 1840 the government took over the canal, and replaced the 40 wooden locks with 27 stone locks ranging in length from 150 to 230 feet with a width of from 26 to 45 feet and 10i feet of water on the sills.-In 1871 this canal was found inadequate and the Welland canal in use at present was begun on a 12 foot basis and then deepened to 14 feet on the sills.- What is known as the present canal was opened in 1887 with 14 feet of water in the sills but it became altogether too small and a more comprehensive scheme was entered upon which is known as the large ship canal. That is the project that is before the country to-day. This the International Joint Commission considers is absolutely necessary if we are to handle the volume of trade which is offering in the West as well as in the East.
As to this ship channel scheme, my hon. friend the member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar), who made a very able speech this afternoon on the subject, and who has evidently been studying the canal problem very deeply, offered some criticism. I do not agree with him when he says there has been no demand for the Welland canal. I well remember the movement which led to its demand. I was president of the Union of Canadian Municipalities which embraces some four hundred and sixty municipalities, and we came down and asked the Borden government for the new Welland ship canal. The deputation was received in the old parliament buildings and we asked the government to go on with this work. At the time there was great congestion of grain on the lakes and congestion generally. The government were launching a second transcontinental railway, and a third was under way. Those that came down on that deputation pointed out the great importance of water-borne traffic in solving the transportation problem of Canada. I may say here that unlike the railways the waterborne traffic has never had a fair chance. The railways have had subsidies, land grants, and handouts of all kinds from governments- from the Dominion government and from the governments of the provinces. The province of Ontario and the old provinces of Upper and Lower Canada have paid a very large proportion of this assistance since confederation. In 1896, I think, there was a return brought down by the Minister of Finance 
which showed that 52 per cent of all the taxes of Canada up to that date had been paid by the old provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Therefore I say there should be no sectional feeling displayed on this question.
The St. Lawrence scheme is one of the most important economic problems we have on the North American continent to-day. We are dependent on the St. Lawrence and the development along the great chain of lakes for future transportation facilities. Therefore I say there was a demand for this particulai work. It was shown there was a great necessity for doing something along this particular line to bring down and regulate rates and give the farmers a chance not only in the West with respect to grain but in many other parts of the country where there was freight to be handled. The government decided to go on with the canal and a very exhaustive inquiry was made and reported on. As a result of that inquiry it was estimated that the cost of the new Welland canal would be about $50,000,000. The minister this afternoon stated it would take $80,000,000 to finish the work, and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle places the probable cost at $100,000,-
000.
I do not agree with that hon. gentleman that the work should have been suspended during the war. I think it was a great mistake that the government suspended the work because it is now going to cost about 50 per cent more than it otherwise would have done. If the contracts had been awarded at the prices for dredging, for concrete work and other classes of work of that description, the contracts being applicable to a period of years, the canal could have been constructed at a saving of twenty-five or thirty million dollars. That was illustrated by the Results which attended similar contracts carried out by the Harbour Commissioners of Toronto. At that time business men and others said "Do not go on with the Toronto harbour improvements, we cannot afford it." The harbour commissioners, however, of whom the late Lieutenant Governor Lionel Clarke, one of the best informed men we had in Canada on the grain situation, was chairman, decided to go ahead with the work. Contracts were awarded to the Canadian Stewart Company on a basis of 191 cents per cubic yard. That work was accomplished during the war and it helped very largely in connection with unemployment. The lands improved were also of a revenue producing character. If that work had not been started at that-time the price would have gone up to 38 or 40 cents a cubic yard, the average rate at present. The work on this Welland

canal, undertaken at this time, is going to cost more money by reason of higher cost of labour, higher cost of materials, the difference in exchange, and everything else than if it had been entered into during the war. To show you the immediate necessity for the building of this canal, I want to refer for a few minutes to the great congestion of the grain elevators. In the West, in North Dakota, and in many other states, this is the case. On both sides of the border the elevators were filled with wheat and could not take in another bushel.

tell us on what terms the United States will co-operate with us in carrying out this work? Have they stated the terms on which they will do it?

terms the United States will do it at the present time. The same thing happens at Montreal.

The rail rate from Buffalo to New York on the published tariff is 9 cents.

Those figures are shown to be wrong, according to this paragraph from the address of J. H. Barnes.
The member for Qu'Appelle says the rate is 6 cents, but Mr. Barnes says:
The rail rate from Buffalo to New York on the published tariff is 9 cents, but as I explained to you prac-

tically no grain was moving. The route that was open -the Erie canal-with totally inadequate facilities advanced the rate to 13 cents per bushel, paralleling the railroad which was supposed to carry it for 9.
From Buffalo to Montreal is a water route. It is equipped with the facilities of forty years ago. It can handle a vessel of 250 feet in length when the lake carrier of to-day west of Buffalo is 600 feet in length. That means that the carriers that operate on this 40-year-old route are limited in number and limited more in carrying capacity. Thirty days ago those carriers were operating on a tariff from Buffalo to Montreal of 6 to 7 cents per bushel. Last Saturday 15J cents was paid for the carriage from Buffalo to Montreal. That is the pressure of grain west of Buffalo seeking an outlet to foreign markets.
The effect of the market rise in prices has been this. In thirty days the foreign price of wheat has advanced 25 cents per bushel, the foreign price of corn has advanced twenty cents per bushel, because these markets are inadequately supplied. The market price in America of wheat has advanced 10 cents per bushel and of corn 10 cents per bushel. That is, the spread between the ultimate foreign price which should be reflected back to our farms, has widened from 10 to 15 cents per bushel because of the lack of adequate facilities to move the crop pressing on the market in the West.
In other words, the lack of a deepened Wei-land canal and adequate rail and water facilities to properly take care of the crop produced the conditions described by Mr. Barnes. These statements I have read from the report of one of the leading experts on the transportation of grain on the North American continent show the necessity of at once deepening this canal, and until the canal is open, the $30,000,000 which has been spent so far has been wasted and will be of no benefit. I think the people of Canada for this reason should get the benefit of the canal as soon as possible. A good many matters have entered into this discussion that I think should not have been brought up, and I was sorry to hear them discussed. In the first place, there has been too much sectional discussion in this chamber regarding this canal. I do not wish to refer to other routes, because they are not relevant to the question before the House. At the same time many of these routes have a great many advantages and disadvantages, and I believe the route via the Welland canal and the river St. Lawrence which has been in existence since 1829 is the best route. The more we discuss it the more we are convinced that it is the logical route for the carriage of grain to the sea.
A question was raised in this debate about the use of the merchant marine and the boats that would be used with the improved Welland canal. I am sorry that these boats have been offered for sale, because I know that there is a good deal of transportation being carried on, not only in package freight, but in the carrying of grain, coal and iron ore that these ships could get.

I will give one concrete example. A company called the Kirkwood Company are now operating between the Maritime provinces and Toronto and Hamilton. Last year this company, with one ship, operated as far west as the cities I have named, and they cut six cents per 100 pounds off the carrying charge for package freight. That had such an effect on the transportation business that the Canada Steamships Company have reduced their rate per 100 pounds, and the Kirkwood Company, according to returns brought down to the House the other day, have written several letters to the government in regard to the purchase of the merchant marine ships. They find they can build up a good trade between the Mother Country and the Maritime provinces and the Great Lakes, through the Welland canal.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) has referred to various matters, but the figures which were presented in the report of the Saskatchewan Grain Commission, in 1914, are not correct, because the prices have been raised; there have been several increases in the rates. The Grain Commission in Saskatchewan sat before the war in 1914, and took evidence. Since that time the cost of transportation between Fort William and Montreal has been fluctuating. The hon. member referred to the average rate as stated in some of the government periodicals. These are not altogether correct in some respects because the quotations in some of the returns for the past two seasons show the rates the hon. member mentioned are not correct. The figures given by the Toronto Harbour Commissioners, and by the commissioners of some other ports on the Great Lakes are at variance with these figures, and I have shown the rates quoted in the report of J. H. Bames from which I have read. The prices to Montreal in the grain congestion last year went up to 13 and 19 cents a bushel. At Buffalo and New York the rates went up in the same ratio. I might say the more you study this particular question the more you will be convinced of the accuracy of my statements. If some hon. members for the West would go down to the banks of the Detroit river in the summertime and spend five or six minutes there, they would see the continual stream of lake freighters of large tonnage passing through. In effect these big freighters all go to Buffalo, because you have no deepened Welland canal to take care of them. The canal is unable to take care of the trade at present. The Erie barge canal cannot take care of the ships and they are delayed there for sixty-

Supply-Canals
days. In effect the Welland canal and lake Ontario route is not able to get the business because of the present small canal. When you take the large freighter the Grant Morden, about 750 feet long, you see what they can do. The grain from that one large ship has to be transferred to seven or eight smaller ships at Port Colborne, in order to take it down lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence. The Wei land canal has never had a chance to show what it can do either in rates or anything else.
In conclusion, I agree with what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has said about the desirability of having additional elevator accommodation all over the Great Lakes; we should have had it long ago. We used to have seven or eight of these elevators in the port from which I come, and there is not a single elevator there now. The farmers of Ontario sent a memorandum to the government some two or three years ago asking for a terminal elevator in central Ontario. We have never got it. When the Welland canal is finished in 1927 there will be a terrible scarcity of elevator accommodation, not only at Port Colborne but at Fort William, Toronto and other cities along the route. It will take several years to build these elevators. Money spent in that direction I think is wisely expended. The natural route for grain is the St. Lawrence and the sooner we get that route in proper shape the more money will be saved in transportation costs and charges.
I wish to read from the International Joint Commission's report one or two conclusions regarding the Welland canal. At page 178, the conclusion of the commission is as follows:
Another factor in the situation that should not bs lost sight of is the peculiar relationship to the proposed improvement of the new Welland ship canal, a portion of which is now under construction. As pointed out in an earlier part of this report, the completion of the Welland ship canal and the adoption and completion of the St. Lawrence improvement would remove the only barrier to the creation of a deepwater route from the head of the lakes to the sea. This would give at least 25-foot navigation from the sea up to the Detroit river, with a present minimum of about 20 feet above Lake Erie. Although entirely outside the strict terms of the reference submitted to it by the two governments, the commission has been impressed by the fact that the new Welland ship canal is such an integral part of the waterway, and is so inseparably interwoven with the project under immediate consideration, that it should properly be considered as a part of the whole scheme and the expense of its construction should be apportioned between the two governments upon the same basis as the works recommended for the upper St. Lawrence.
About a page or so further on they recommend :
That the new Welland ship canal be embodied in said scheme and treated as a part thereof.
That Canada proceed with the works necessary for the completion of said new Welland ship canal in accordance with the plans already decided upon by that country.
I want to say to hon. gentlemen from the West that I believe the people of Ontario are sympathetic to the desire that the West should receive increased transportation facilities, not only by rail, but by water, and they want to see the West grow and prosper. The hope of the country is in the West. They want to see the West receive a measure of relief from the transportation difficulties they have in that great country to-day. With the early completion of the Welland ship canal, all the great boats on the upper lakes will be able to go down to lake Ontario, and this will bring about, not only a cut in the rates, but a more important factor, namely relief from the congestion of the railways and assistance in getting the crop out. It will do a great deal to reduce costs and will assist the farmers as well.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) dwelt on the cost of this canal and many other phases of the problem. The figures fluctuate very much. The interests of the country would be best served by the immediate construction of this canal. In conclusion, I hope the work will be started this year, and that a vigorous effort will be made by the engineers in charge to push it along. The engineers who had charge of the Chippawa power canal had their own plant; they had an electrically driven shovel and other electrical devices of all kinds; the engineering was modem throughout, and they did a great deal of the work themselves, with the result that a great work like that was consummated with very considerable economy.

I do not know whether any serious objection can be taken to the expenditure on the Welland ship canal at the present time. I think the objection should have been taken some years ago. I do not know whether the last speaker (Mr. Church) spoke wisely and said the truth -when he said that 830,000,000 had already been wasted. But the question that I wish to ask at this period is this; What will be the value of the canal when it is completed, if it is looked upon as a unit? I have listened to the various arguments that have been presented in this House this afternoon, and all who have spoken in favour of the Welland canal did so in the light of the larger scheme, in conjunction, I might say, with the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway. If the Welland canal has no virtue outside of the larger scheme.

it seems to me that at the present time it would be opportune to object to the expenditure (hat is now being advocated. The argument in favour of both schemes is this, that grain and other commodities will be carried much more cheaply. As regards grain, we heard this afternoon that the grain would have to be handled at least five or six times before it reached Montreal for shipment to Great Britain. I can hardly understand how you are going to cheapen rates when you have to handle a commodity five or six times before it reaches the ultimate consumer.
The question that confronts us at the present time is this: In view of the larger scheme, can we seriously contemplate the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway when we consider that we have only 9,000,000 people, those people already well over-burdened with taxation? Before that scheme can really be contemplated, we need a much larger population and a great deal more work for the canal to do. Are we really utilizing the resources that we now have? The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) said that when he was in the West in company with the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the West was advocating the deepening of the Welland canal. I was wondering at that particular time whether the West had three transcontinental railways that were not being fully utilized, or whether they were even completed. But the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) spoke rightly when he said that we had three great transcontinental railways and that we were not utilizing them to the fullest advantage. As a people we believe in economy. Why should we not utilize these railways to their greatest effect, and then if they prove inadequate, to stop the shortage or to meet any embarrassment we find in the fall season, it will be quite time for us to advocate some larger scheme? I should like the minister to say, after I am through, if there is any virtue in the Welland canal if it is taken by itself, whether it will be of any benefit to the West, or to any other part of the country if the St. Lawrence waterway scheme is never completed.
As regards the cost, the hon. member (Mr. Church) said that if we had continued the work during the war, the cost would have been SO per cent greater. The minister himself said that when the canal was started, it was expected to cost $55,000,000. He then went on to say that it may cost eighty or ninety million dollars, and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle says possibly $100,000,000, which figure, I think, is more nearly correct. In that case, although the war did stop the work, we find that the

work is costing 100 per cent more than it was originally expected to cost. How much of the work is completed? Last year the late Minister of Railways gave us a detailed statement regarding the expenditure, the contracts that were under way, and we would be glad to have that information now.
As regards the larger scheme, I understood from the hon. member (Mr. Church) that the United States were willing to build the canal, that is the canal from lake Ontario to Montreal. I have carefully read many of the statements that have appeared in our papers, and I have never heard or read of any public man, any official, stating that the United States were willing to pay for this great scheme. If that is so, I would be glad to be corrected in my statement; but I do mot believe such a statement has been made, and until we in this country have been able to pay some part of the principal of our war debt, until we as a people are willing to live within our own budget and taxation which we are able to impose upon the people, it is presumptuous for anyone to advocate a scheme that will involve this young country with a small population in an expenditure of possibly over $300,000,000. For that reason, before I can vote intelligently upon a scheme on which possibly some $35,000,000 has already been expended, I want the minister to inform me how much work has been completed, what contracts have been let for this year, and what the cost of the entire scheme completed will amount to.
My hon. friend intimated that it would have been better to go on with the work during the war-
No.
-because it would have been cheaper. Does he realize that this would have meant cutting down the wages of the men to 50 per cent of what they are getting now.
I do not think I said that. I said that at the present time the work is costing 100 per cent more than it would have amounted to under pre-war prices.

If my hon. friend did not mean what I said then I accept his explanation. But I understood him to argue that it would have been wiser to go on with the work at that time because we could have got it done more cheaply. It was impossible to go on with the contracts. They were made on the 1913 basis and the contractors accepted the fair wage clause under which the men would have to be paid the current rate of wages, and during the war the current rate of

wages was more than double what it was before. The only thing that could have been . done during the war was to devote all the energies of the country to the prosecution of our part in the struggle, and these other things had to be dropped for the time being. I do not see how the late government could have done anything else.
As to the other question, of the United States offering to build their share of the canal, this matter was discussed by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) before six o'clock, when he said that it had been recommended by the International Joint Commission that the United States should pay a certain proportion of the cost. The United States, however, have not accepted that proposition, although it has been recommended. As regards the benefit to be derived from the Welland canal, as I said this afternoon, you cannot make any absolute statement. If the enlargement of the Welland canal, apart altogether from the larger scheme, is not going to be a factor in lowering transportation costs, then undoubtedly the expenditure on it would be a foolish one. But is it not reasonable to suppose that if the larger bulk of traffic can be carried 200 miles nearer to ocean-going vessels and then be transshipped, it must of necessity lessen the cost of the entire carriage? Let me illustrate the point. It is only a matter of hours, for instance, to transfer a cargo from Prescott or Kingston to Montreal for ocean transportation, while if these smaller vessels have to come all the way from Port Colborne, or 200 miles further away, the cost, as my hon. friend can well see, is bound to be increased. In other words, the closer you can get a cargo in large bulk to the point of final shipment the cheaper must be the freight rates. If there were never to be a further deepening of the St. Lawrence channel the enlargment of the Welland canal must be of benefit to the solution of the transportation problem in the way of reducing costs. As a matter of fact, the surveys for the enlargement of the Welland canal were undertaken and were partially complete before the larger scheme was seriously thought of; and it has been contended, and will be accepted as a truism by all men who have studied the question, that the deepening of the canal, allowing larger ships to come to the end of deep water above the rapids, must tend to reduce the cost of transportation.
No new contracts have been let this year. As I pointed out this afternoon, sections 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 are under construction, while 6, 7, and 8 have not yet been let. The object is to have the contracts let so that the completion of the work on all the contracts will be accomplished approximately about the same time. As to the percentages of work done, earth excavation has been completed to the extent of 48 per cent; watertight embankments, 60 per cent; rock excavation, 31 per cent; concrete excavation, 31 per cent; and reinforcing walls, about 40 per cent. That is for the whole of the contracts.

I was struck with the minister's statement before six o'clock in regard to the strong representations made from the West for the Welland canal; and the same thing has been repeated by the hon. member (Mr. Church) to-night. I remember very well when the minister made his trip throughout the West along with the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, but I cannot recall any concrete demand for the Welland canal at that time. I am probably speaking from the producers' standpoint rather than from the standpoint of a representative of some of the corporations or municipalities which the hon. gentleman has spoken of. However, it has occurred to me that if the minister wishes to satisfy the demand of the West in the matter of railway transportation he will be afforded a very good opportunity when he brings down that estimate he has promised for the Hudson Bay railway. I do not want to precipitate a discussion on that item just now, because no doubt we shall have occasion later to deal with it; and the liberal estimate which appears here for the Welland canal encourages me to look forward to equally generous provision for the completion of the Hudson Bay route. I question very much, though, whether we are justified in voting so much money for the Welland canal at the present time. I endorse most heartily what was said by the member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) this afternoon, in regard to some of the matters he discussed. He stated, I believe, that so far as he could figure out the completion of the Welland canal would make no more difference to the transportation of grain than possibly 2 cents per bushel. Personally I doubt whether it would make even that much difference. But I think the minister would be well advised to consider some of the other demands that have come forward.
Is my hon. friend in a position to tell us by how much the completion of the Hudson Bay railway would decrease the cost of freight? We must have definite information.

The information in this regard will be just as definite as it can be in connection with the other matter. We know from

the report submitted by the Lake Freights commission that the rates last year from September to November varied all the way from 3 to 11 cents, and while we have such conditions we can form no idea of the cost of carrying grain from Fort William to Montreal. We know in regard to the Hudson Bay route, taking Saskatoon as a centre, that grain can be carried to Port Nelson for less than it can be carried to Fort William, and we also know that Port Nelson is approximately as near Liverpool as is Montreal. If we can eliminate the cost of lake transportation along with considerable rail transportation there is no doubt that the saving on that route would be very much more than the saving that would be gained by the deepening of the Welland canal. I shall not continue the discussion now because, as I said before, I am iooking forward to a very liberal estimate being brought down for this work shortly, and then we will have an opportunity to discuss it further.

Mr. Chairman, I am somewhat surprised to find hon. members from the West opposing the completion of the Welland canal, for I have the conviction that the development of the St. Lawrence route is the very best undertaking that can be carried out in the interests of the grain growers of the West. It will s-ecure for them a reduction in the cost of carrying their grain to the seaboard that is variously estimated at from 7 to 12 cents a bushel. My hon. friend from Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) seems to argue that before we think of improving our transportation routes we should congest all our railway routes with grain.

How does my hon. friend
estimate the saving of from 7 to 12 cents a bushel on the transportation of grain by the improvement of the Welland canal and the deepening of the St. Lawrence?

I am not putting that forward as my own estimate, but on the authority of men who have gone into the question very thoroughly, such as the engineers of the International Joint Commission. It is their estimate.

Does the hon. member refer
to the deepening of the Welland canal or of the St. Lawrence?

I say that when you get
the water route from the head of the lakes to Montreal or Quebec available for the through transport of grain a saving on the cost of transportation will be effected which is estimated at from 7 to 12 cents per bushel.

Considering that even last
season when there was a great deal of congestion and a monopoly was operating on the Great Lakes a considerable quantity of wheat was carried for less than 12 cents a bushel, how does my hon. friend arrive at his estimate that 12 cents a bushel could be saved between Fort William and Montreal?

I think my hon. friend will find that that rate was secured for only two or three cargoes and that it is capable of explanation, but not being conversant with the circumstances I cannot explain such an exceptionally low rate. I do not think any one will attempt to argue that it is not cheaper to carry grain by water from the head of the lakes to Quebec than by lake and rail. It is notorious that the cost of carrying any merchandise by rail is greater than by water. My idea is that the work on the Welland canal should be proceeded with with all possible energy and that the other part of the great water system from the head of the lakes to Quebec should be completed.
In reply to my hon. friend from Swift Current who estimates the improvement of the St. Lawrence channel at $300,000,000, I would point out that he is about $50,000,000 higher than the estimate made by very competent authorities of the International Joint Commission. But there is this factor to be kept in mind, that by improving the St. Lawrence channel we would get a by-product which would pay for the whole cost of the work. That fact was brought out last session, I think, by my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) with some very definite and convincing figures. The electrical energy to be developed along with the improvement of the channel could be made to pay for the whole undertaking, and if we adopted Mr. Gardiner's plan of financing this enterprise, all that the Dominion would be committed to would be a guarantee of its share of the cost of the work. In a book written by him on the St. Lawrence deep waterways Mr. Gardiner, of Chicago, proposes that the government of Canada and the government of the United States should jointly appoint an international commission with authority to issue bonds. It was Mr. Gardiner's opinion that three times the amount of money required for the work could be raised at 4 per cent, it would be such an attractive investment. According to his idea the commission would operate the undertaking without profit. No doubt the commissioners would be properly remunerated for their work but there would be no dividends to pay, and what would usually be diverted for this purpose would go to amortize the debt. So that

all the responsibility the Dominion would incur would be the guarantee of its share of the bonds. It follows that the financing of the undertaking would be a very easy proposition, and when the work was completed we would have a deep waterway from Fort William to the city of Quebec, or perhaps lower down, where great cargoes could be transshipped and we would reduce to a minimum the cost of handling the grain from the producer on the prairies to the consumer in Europe. We have vessels now carrying 500,000 bushels-

bushels.

Well, I was putting it well within the mark. One of these great freighters from Fort William could take 500,000 bushels of grain down to Quebec-not stopping at Montreal necessarily, except that this port has great elevator capacity

or even down to the gulf, and there transship its cargo to two or three tramp steamers which would take it across the ocean. I venture to say that the greatest relief for the agricultural industry in western Canada is to be obtained in that way. I voted for the Hudson Bay railway.
I do not believe that that route is going to give the farmers of the West so much relief as they expect, for I am afraid the navigation season will be too short. What I do pin my faith to is the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence deep waterway, and I think my hon. friends who live in the West, and whose interest lies in getting their produce to the world's markets at the lowest cost, should not oppose the spending of money on any link of that great waterway which will ultimately-and shortly, I venture to say-be completed. I do not think there is enough influence anywhere to prevent this project being undertaken and carried to completion, because it is one of nature's great waterways, and only requires to be developed to give its full service to this country. I believe that when Canada can join with the United States to carry out this great international work there will be such a flood of trade through our lakes and down the St. Lawrence that it will astonish the people of this country. If my memory is right, I have seen it stated somewhere that of the grain produced on our western prairies last year less than 40 per cent went by Montreal, the bulk of it, or 60 per cent, going out by Buffalo. There is no reason on earth why 60 per cent of our grain should go out by a foreign channel, especially when we have better means for its transportation, but the big barges on the Erie canal have been taking this large percentage of our wheat to

New York and developing that port at the expense of our own ports. I think, Sir, that of all classes of our people those who stand to gain most by the development of our waterways from lake Erie to the gulf of St. Lawrence are the men who grow grain on the western prairies.

Nearly every hon. member who has spoken on this vote has coupled the deepening of the Welland canal with the completion of the St. Lawrence deep waterway.
Although the minister has given his 9 p.m. view as to the reason why the Welland canal should be finished, I believe that the full benefit of the new Wellard canal will not be available until the St. Lawrence route is completed. On May 29 last year the Prime Minister, in response to a question from the hon. member for West York, said that a reply had been sent to the United States government that this was not an opportune time to discuss this question, particularly as the report from the International Joint Commission had only been available for a short time. That objection is disposed of now, of course, by the lapse of time.
It seems to me that this discussion has revolved a great deal around the transportation of wheat and the problem of getting the wheat from the western prairies out to the seaboard. There are many routes proposed. The route by way of Vancouver has been dealt with previously this session, and a large amount was voted for the construction of an elevator at Vancouver harbour, which will no doubt take care of a great deal of the wheat at the western end of the prairies. The hon. member for Prince Albert is in hopes that the Hudson Bay railway will also transport a great deal of western wheat. It seems to me that the production of wheat in Canada is by no means limited. We have not yet reached the maximum production, and even with all these increased facilities for shipment we shall not be able to handle the crops which are to come any better than those we have handled in the past. The development of the St. Lawrence waterway is not entirely for the purpose of shipping grain. There is also involved in it the question of supplying fuel for Ontario particularly. Recently we have been making efforts to get a favourable freight rate on western coal, but the only rate available, $9 per ton, seems too high for us to be able to bring western coal to Ontario. There therefore remains the St. Lawrence route, which in time will possibly mean that Nova Scotia coal or coke can be delivered in Ontario at competitive prices with the American product, or it may be that

Welsh coal, which found its way last winter as far as Brantford, Ontario, coming from Montreal by rail, will be enabled to come up the St. Lawrence river and into lake Ontario and perhaps lake Huron.
Another object which we have in view is the development of power. About twelve years ago the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario undertook to sell 10,000 horsepower in the municipalities adjoining the Niagara district. The chairman of that commission was told that he would never find a market for 10,000 horse-power, but in a few years the demand had so increased that it reached 275,000 horse-power, and the existing plants being worked to capacity it was necessary to provide further development, and the Chippawa creek scheme was launched with a plant first of all with a capacity of
100,000	horse-power. Ten million dollars was to have been spent on that development, but the demand for power increased by leaps and bounds, and in the end that development is to reach an estimated production of 600,000 horse-power and cost about $80,000,000. Now we are told that if the demand within the next three or four years increases in the same proportion, all the power that is being developed at the Chippawa plant will be taken and virtually all the power that can be developed in the Niagara district will then be utilized; and it will be available at prices ranging from one-half to one-third of the cost at which power can be developed by the use of coal. In my own city of London, which is about 120 miles from Niagara, we contracted about ten years ago for, I think it was, 4,000 horse-power. Some of those who were opposed to the scheme threw up their hands and asked: What will you do? You will never get rid of it. But the result is that the city is now using four times that amount and is calling for more. Niagara power is now being distributed throughout the rural districts. The farmers are beginning to use it, and that demand is going to increase very largely. So, Mr. Chairman, it will be necessary for Ontario to find more power somewhere.
The report of the United States and Canadian engineers on the St. Lawrence development goes to show that about 1,500,000 horsepower can be developed in connection with the construction of this deep waterway, and that probably 3,000,000 additional horse-power can be developed in time. I support most heartily the suggestion of the hon. member for Welland that the United States government be invited to a conference on this question. They came to us asking us to meet 
them in a conference to discuss the terms of a treaty, but there is no reason why Canada cannot counter with a different proposition. Terms may be discussed, and as the hon. member for Swift Current suggested, the ideas of the United States legislators could be secured on the proposition.
Many figures have been quoted as to what the scheme would mean in the saving of freight on wheat. I have a clipping here which I cut from the Toronto Globe of November 14, 1922. It gives the opinion of Governor J. A. Preus of Minnesota who was in Ottawa about that time. He estimated that there would be a saving of 7i cents per bushel on grain shipped from Duluth to Liverpool by the proposed St. Lawrence deep waterway. He said:
This amount was spread over the short railway haulage from Buffalo to New York. The total cost of shipping to Liverpool from Duluth was 15J cents a bushel. All the fanners of eighteen states bordering on the Great Lakes were anxious to have the St. Lawrence deep waterway constructed as soon as possible. Railway transportation in the United States was very inadequate. Potatoes were rotting in the ground in Minnesota and western states because farmers could not get enough cars to handle their crops.
The only opposition to the scheme in the United States came from the New England states and New York.
Recent newspaper reports would lead one to believe that many of the railroads in the central states are also favourable to this development. I would like to ask if the government has had any communication from the Ontario provincial government or the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission relative to this project being taken up as a provincial activity.

I cannot speak positively as to that. The chairman of the Hydro Electric Commission, Sir Adam Beck, had one or two conversations with me concerning it, but there were merely suggestions, no definite statement was made as to the province taking up the project on its own initiative altogether. I can scarcely see how the province itself could undertake the entire work because it is so interwoven with the federal situation both in the United States and Canada, but we did have a discussion as to the possibilities of the project. In fact, Sir Adam Beck suggested a partial development of the undertaking for the present, but as to the details of how this should be done I think there was nothing definite said.

There seems to be some opposition among our friends from the West to the expenditure of money on deepening the Welland canal. I believe that there

To-day the trade amounts to very little. The large bulk of it, during the last few years, has been going to the United States-We believe that the deepening of the Welland canal, in addition to reducing the freight rate, will restore this traffic again to our Canadian ports, to our own Canadian steamship lines and to our own Canadian railways.

I would not have taken part in this debate at the present time were it not for the assumption contained in the speeches of some hon. gentlemen, an assumption which I am prepared to admit is warranted in some degree because of speeches made from this comer of the House, that the West is unanimously opposed to the project of the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterways. In spite of the fact that last year, in speaking on this matter, I indicated some doubt as to whether the time is opportune for engaging in the expenditure necessary in that great work, I did express the opinion that the time would come when that work would be a completed fact. Indeed, I feel satisfied that in the not very distant future it will be an accomplished fact. In regard to the Welland canal itself I confess that I had some doubts as to the wisdom of continuing expenditure on that work until the greater project itself was well under way. I may say, however, that in view of the discussion this afternoon, and some thought I had given it previously, I can see that while the full benefit of the Welland canal will not be available until the greater work is completed, there is reason to believe that even with the one link connecting lake Erie with lake Ontario, thus making it possible to bring the grain farther down in the larger vessels, there is reason to believe that there can be a considerable saving effected in the carriage of wheat.
