Some few years ago, going back to the larger project, I attended a conference in Winnipeg at which the hon. member for Welland was present together with a number of gentlemen from the United States. I was there representing our farmers' organization at that time. They placed the matter very fully before us, and from that time I have been very sympathetically disposed towards the larger enterprise. It is true we laid down two propositions at that time. We refused to accept it as an alternative to the Hudson Bay railway, nor do I think there is any disposition indicated here to offer it as an alternative. We take it that those members who have spoken from all sides of the House have spoken in good faith when they have said that the Hudson Bay railway will be completed. However, we did lay down that proposition, and we also laid down another: That we could not agree to the expenditure of a large sum of money on the part of Canada until there was some assurance that the benefits that would come, or that should come, to Canada by entering into that larger scheme would not be absorbed by some lake freight shippers combine. I think the fear we expressed on that occasion was well warranted, as was amply demonstrated during last fall which led to government action in the appointment of a royal commission, the report of which is now before the country. Undoubtedly the necessity has been made manifest of having the rates under some control. I will just say again that I have no desire to enter into a lengthy discussion at the present time. I for one would just like to make it known that the West is not absolutely opposed to this scheme as might seem to be implied by some of the things that have been said.

Before the vote carries
there are one or two observations I should like to make further in regard to this matter. In speaking of the construction of the St. Lawrence deep waterways, the estimated cost of which is $250,000,000, certain hon. gentlemen made the statement that that estimate will not nearly complete the work. They say it will cost double that and they instance the fact that the construction of the new Welland ship canal has cost, or will cost, nearly double the estimated amount of its construction, I should like to call attention of hon. gentlemen to this fact:	The estimated cost of the Welland ship canal was $55,000,000. That was in pre-war times. The canal is divided for construction purposes into eight sections. Four of those sections were advertised prior to the war, and three of

them are among the heaviest construction sections on the canal. Yet the tenders for these four sections were all within the estimate. The tenders on which the contracts were made, were within the engineer's estimates for construction. If the whole work had been tendered for as advertised and contracts entered into for its construction previous to the war, those contracts would have all been at prices within the engineer's estimates. The war came on and we all know what happened. I wish to call the attention of hon. members to the further fact that the engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals who made the estimate for the construction of the Welland canal is the same engineer, or one of the same engineers, who made the estimate for the construction of the St. Lawrence deep waterway, and instead of that estimate being made on pre-war prices, it was made during the continuance of the War and at prices which prevailed at that time, and consequently when he estimates a icost of $252,000,000 or thereabouts for the construction of the deep waterway from lake Ontario to Montreal it is based on the estimate of cost which is above what that cost would be at the present time. So that I will venture to say that the work can be done well within the engineer's estimate. But even at that, in view of the financial conditions of the country at the present time, I would not stand up and speak in favour of the construction of this channel if I did not feel absolutely convinced in my own mind that the work could be done and paid for by the disposal of the electric current which will be developed by reason of that construction. Now, $252,000,000 will not only construct the deep channel from lake Ontario to Montreal, but it will also pay for the construction of the hydraulic plant which will develop at the Long Sault rapids 1,500,000 electric horsepower, one half of which or 750,000 electrical horse-power will belong to Canada. That can be sold at the switch board of the power house retail at $14 per horse-power. Yes, and more than that; because at this very hour hydro-electric power developed at Niagara Falls is costing in the Niagara district $20 per horse-power. The price has gone up by reason of the extra cost of construction, and it is costing us in the city of Welland at this hour $20 per horse-power. So that when I say this horse-power can be sold at the switch board for $14 per horse-power it is well within the mark, and 750,000 horse-power at $14 per horse-power will in thirty-five or forty years pay every dollar of the cost of construction of that St. Lawrence deep waterway.

Supply-Canals
It is not a million and a half horse-power?

I would like if the hon.
member could give the pro rata values, or what price is charged in urban districts and in rural districts for power?
The hon. member means in Ontario?
Yes.

Exactly the same price -no difference. It is "service at cost" in Ontario, and what it costs to produce and transmit is what the consumer pays, no matter where it may be located. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) says it is not a million and a half horse-power. It is a million and a half for the whole development, 750,000 of which would be for Canada.
That is only on the international waterways.
That is only on the international section. Of course another 2,000,000 horse-power can be developed on the remaining sections of the river between the Long Sault rapids and Montreal.
All in Canada.

Yes, every bit of it. The minister has stated that there was a question as to the legal right to use the St. Lawrence river, as between the province of Ontario and the Dominion. I do not think it will serve any useful purpose at the present time to discuss the relative legal rights of the province and the Dominion regarding the use of the waters of the St. Lawrence. I will venture to make this statement and express this opinion-it is only an opinion, and I will be interested in knowing what the newspapers, at any rate in Ontario, think about it-that the people of the province of Ontario are so anxious that this St. Lawrence project should not only be begun, but prosecuted energetically and immediately, that they would be willing, even though they had the legal right to the whole of it, to allow the proceeds of the sale of the 750,000 horse-power which is to be developed to be applied first in payment of the cost of construction, and after that payment has been accomplished that the proceeds of the sale of that power should be handed over to the province, if it was found that the province was solely and wholly entitled to it.

Does the hon. member mean the entire construction? He does not want us to understand that he is distinguishing between the cost that is attributable to the benefit of navigation and the cost that is attributable to power?

I was not distinguishing between them at all. I say that I believe that the people of Ontario would be willing that the proceeds of the sale of the 700,000 electrical horse-power which can be developed should be applied first to paying Canada's share of the whole cost of the construction of the deep water channel from lake Ontario to Montreal, which would be $125,000,000.
Where would you sell it?

That question is being asked by many people, "Where would you sell it? There is no market." It is only a very few years ago, perhaps 20 years ago, that electric power was developed at Niagara Falls. I heard that same question asked at that time. "Where can you sell 100,000 horse-power "? I was told by the then Premier of Ontario that we could not sell
30.000	horse-power. I told him that in a very few years we would not only be selling 30,000 electric horse-power, but we would be selling
300.000	electric horse-power, and these words have not only come true, but more than come true, because at this hour, after 20 years of the use of the electric current developed at Niagara Falls, we are disposing in this province, from Niagara Falls only, of 500,000 electric horse-power, and the people are crying for more. That 700,000 electric horse-power would be sold, certainly inside of ten years, and I believe inside of five years. There is no question about disposing of this commodity. If you read the information which is given in the report of the International Joint Commission, you will find that, after a thorough investigation, they say that far and away more than that will be disposed of in a short time. Therefore, I say that there will be no difficulty about the sale and there should be no difficulty about the beginning and the continuance of the construction of that great enterprise.
Those of us who are members of the Canadian Deep Waterways and Power Association are not asking the government to pledge themselves to anything. We are asking them to do only what, in my opinion, is a gentlemanly thing to do. The United States government first communicated with the government of Canada asking them to a conference. The government of Canada said: "No, we cannot have a conference with you now; it is too early." We ask the government now, after nearly two years of office, to say: "Now, we will sit down and discuss this matter with
Supply-Canals

you." Ask them to a conference this time. They asked you a while ago for reciprocity. You ignored that request. You did not wait for them to ask you again; you are asking them now for reciprocity. Therefore I say: They asked you for a conference over this St. Lawrence waterways scheme. You refused it. Now sit down and ask them to join you in a conference- discuss the matter, and if you find that the estimates of the engineers are correct, and that there is a reasonable chance of disposing of the electric current which can be developed, then go ahead with this project which will be a benefit to the whole community.

I quite understand the hon. member's state of mind when he says that nobody is asking this government to pledge itself to anything. That is a very general attitude. I feel that I should say something, and this time in support of the contention advanced by the minister, that is, in support of the appropriation, irrespective for the time being of the larger project. The history of the Welland canal development, that is, of this last improvement, dates to about the beginning or before the beginning of the war. The project was continued until war necessities compelled its suspension. It was resumed as soon as possible after, in order that we might, as quickly as we could, arrive at the day when the large amount of capital already invested would be making some return. We felt that we could not launch on a very large scale on the renewed prosecution; but we did put in what we thought were reasonable appropriations, considering the circumstances of the time. Following exactly the same policy, the minister puts in now a similar appropriation.
It cannot be argued successfully that the deepening of the Welland canal will have value only when the larger project is complete. If such were the case, then it would be just as cheap to carry grain from Fort William in the canal vessels that now pass through right to Montreal. What I mean is this: If it were as cheap to carry grain over that distance from the Welland canal to Prescott or Kingston in small vessels as in large, certainly there never would have been any deepening at all. We might just as well take the small vessels right on to Fort William. In a word, if it is possible to carry in large vessels the distance from Fort William through the Sault to the Welland canal, though that entails a transfer into small vessels there, how much more will it pay to carry in large vessels 210 miles more, say to 
Prescott, when no extra transfer at all is entailed? One cannot, if one simply stops there, argue the question any further. Undoubtedly the further you take the grain in the large vessels, the cheaper the transportation. How much cheaper it would be, it may be hard to estimate; but if it is only two cents or a cent and a half, then undoubtedly there is value, even though we do not contemplate that the canal is to be ultimately part of a larger scheme.
It is quite true that if, after we have the best means of transportation, the grip of an ocean syndicate is going to demand whatever figure it likes, we might as well go back and rely upon our railways. We have to have competition, or if we cannot have competition, we must have control. The business of government is to get the best method of transport. That is the basic necessity. After that the matter is one of government; the enterprise feature is over. You must first, though, get the best method of transport. We cannot argue that we should leave it to our railroads.
Water transportation has always had an immense advantage over land transportation, and the advantage, instead of diminishing in proportion, has really been increasing. It is now estimated, I think, and I think very accurately estimated, that the proportion of cost at present rates is about one to ten. What I mean to say is this: Taking the actual investment, cost of carriage, cost of upkeep and all the rest, it is just about one to ten; you can carry about ten miles by water what you can carry one mile by land. The advantage of the water over the land has increased with increased capital investment necessary for railways-of course we have that already- with increased cost of upkeep, increased wages, increased cost of material. Very well; it follows that with that tendency the value of our waterways right into the heart of this Dominion and this continent as a transportation asset multiplies with the years. It is a tremendous asset to this country. When we get it utilized as it can be, we bring the products of the East right into the very heart of the American continent by the largest vessels. Consequently we must first make the best transport lines we can, and having done that, of course government is necessary. There may be a change of government necessary before we reap the harvest, but those things can be attended to in due course.

We are not going to delay the work that long.

Supply-Canals
The work necessary to a change will be undertaken even before the completion.
Naturally.

Very naturally. The completion of the change will follow quickly upon the undertaking. I was going to refer, though, to opposition apparently developing, not unanimously, but in some degree, from western Canada to this route. I think that is a mistake; I think hon. members will live to regret that they have assumed this attitude.
I have never opposed, indeed I have urged, the completion of the Hudson Bay railway. I have urged it more as a matter of honest contractual obligation to western Canada than based on any certain assurance in my mind that it is bound to be a commercial success.
I say here and now that I would rather stake what little reputation I have upon the value of the investment in the Welland canal than upon the value of any investment in the Hudson Bay road. Twenty years, thirty years from now, those who support the water route right out through our Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence will, in my judgment, have more reason to be proud of their record than those who were very enthusiastic over the Hudson Bay road. Nevertheless, the latter road must as soon as we can complete it, be completed; it would be folly to desist. We had in our estimates of 1921, that is for 1921-22, $5,000,000 odd, perhaps $5,000,000 only, to carry on this Welland canal wark. We were pretty bitterly abused. The lovetaps now administered to the hon. minister in charge of the estimates are very mild compared with the flogging we had to take for daring to do our duty in regard to the same enterprise. Indeed, in the campaign of 1921,1 want to remind hon. members, when I challenged the leader of the Progressive party to make good by specific articles the charge of wild extravagance against the government of that time, the first thing he pointed to was $5,000,000 on the Welland canal. That was the most outstanding instance of folly he could think of. We have now $11,000,000 and though there is objection it is not very strong. I venture to say that the objection will get less and less, and that with the opening up of real prospects through our waterway navigation the country will grow in unanimity behind the scheme.

Before the vote carries I
think it only well that I should make a few additional remarks since considerable reference has been made to what I said this afternoon. I agree with every word
the leader of the Opposition said until he came to the point where he referred to the comparison between water rates and rail rates. Looking over an American report I noticed that the comparison was nine to one Borne years ago in favour of water rates on the lakes. Since that time a great change has taken place. If it is ten to one now how is it that the railways from BuSalo to New York have put the Erie canal out of business?

The Erie canal is not
a really practicable waterway at all. It is a 12-foot water route, and you cannot carry heavy traffic on such a canal.
Mr. GRAHAM. And it is not all of that depth.
No; it is not much better than a ditch.

It is only a few years
since the Erie canal was deepened to 12 feet. It was only 8 feet until recently, and even now it is not 12 feet all the way.

Well, let us take another
case. The Canadian Pacific Railway carries grain from Calgary' to Fort William, which distance I have heard variously stated at 1,280 and 1,290 miles, for 151 cents, whereas on the water route from Fort William to Montreal, a distance of about 1,200 miles, there have been as many as 22 different rates. The rates varied a great deal last season between these two points. I think that what would be considered a fair rate at present would be close to 10 or 11 cents. As a matter of fact I was slightly in error this afternoon when I stated that I thought 11 cents a fair rate. What I really intended to say was. that this was an estimate I had seen stated for purposes of argument. I consider 11 cents really too high, and yet the distance for which this charge is made is some 1,200 miles as against the other rate I have cited of 1,280 miles.

Just in order to clear the point, I might explain to my hon. friend that the rate from the head of the lakes to Montreal is largely consumed in trans'-shipments at the Georgian bay ports, or at Port Col-bome. I understood my right. hon. friend's estimate to refer to clear open-water transportation such as out in the lakes or on the ocean, but in a canal system the rate is naturally enhanced.

I think the hon. member
(Mr. Manion) is putting the case too strongly when he says that a large part of the expense is taken up in the way he suggests. A little of it is consumed that way, but not a large per-
37S8
Supply-Canals

centage. Let me refer to another remark made by the leader of the Opposition and by the member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). They both seem to infer from the discussion that some of the western members at least are opposed to the deepening of the Welland canal and of the St. Lawrence. I do not know of anyone who is opposed to the undertaking. The remarks I have made and those I have heard have been directed to the question as to when it would be wise to complete the work. That is all; and in order to arrive at a conclusion on that point we have been discussing the advantage that we might gain as shippers of grain, and how much we should save per bushel. I am quite confident the time will come when the St. Lawrence route will be deepened, and properly so; and it is quite well that the Welland canal should also be completed, especially in view of the fact that it has been started. I can agree with some hon. members, however, that it was started too soon, and it is now a question how quickly we ought to complete it.
Reference was made by some hon. members to the amount that would be saved, and the estimates vary from 7i cents from the governor of Minnesota to 12 cents. Dealing with the high estimate that was suggested of 11 cents from Fort William to Montreal, I divided the cost into two parts: one was 4J cents as far as Port Colbome and the other 7 cents from Port Colbome to Montreal. Now, it is readily seen that the only saving after the St. Lawrence route is opened up and the Welland canal is completed will be effected between Port Colborne and Montreal, I think that 7 cents is a very high estimate; it is far more than the grain will be carried for. But how will you save 12 cents when it is obvious that the total cost of carrying it is 7 cents as I have shown? That is what I want the committee to understand before this parliament commits the country to an expenditure of $252,000,000, which, as in a great many public undertakings, might probably be doubled in the long run. The member for Welland (Mr. German) suggested that it was probable we should not have to expend a dollar; he suggested that it would not cost the Canadian people one cent.

Where will they get
the money?

We have often heard that story. When something is promoted it is suggested that we are going to get something for nothing, but I do not think anyone will be foolish enough to be caught by that sort of thing now. Who thinks that if we deepen the St. Lawrence at a cost of two or three hundred

million dollars the Canadian people will not have to shoulder any of that cost? It seems hardly worth serious consideration. Let us rest assured that when the St. Lawrence river is deepened Canada will pay for it and pay more than $252,000,000. The hon. member (Mr. Church) stated that my figures were not correct. That can be readily explained; as I said a moment ago, the rates are constantly varying. There were twenty-two different rates between various points last season, so I think hon. members will realize that by taking certain rates on specified dates one can prove almost anything. The rates I took were average rates, so I think my statement stands.

I have been somewhat interested by remarks made by hon. gentlemen concerning this item. The Welland canal is getting to be quite a hardy annual and we look for its recurrence year after year, although it is pleasing to note that the appropriation is smaller this year and we hope that eventually it will disappear altogether. The statement I am about to make is not in opposition to the Welland canal and I am merely using this work as a key to the larger project which has entered into the discussion, namely, the deepening of the St. Lawrence route. I have taken the figures submitted by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) and made a few calculations. Taking a capitalization of approximately $250,000,000-and I might preface my remarks by referring to the prediction of certain hon. gentlemen that the power development and so on would pay for the whole undertaking-taking this capitalization, Canada's share is $125,000,000, which at 5 per cent-I have increased the interest rate- gives an interest charge of $6,250,000, which would have to come out of the revenue received from the sale of 750,000 horse power at $14 per horse power, or $10,500,000. Deducting from this revenue our bond interest charge of $6,250,000, we have a balance of $4,250,000. As business men, I do not think we would be prepared to deny that it would take the whole of this balance every year to meet the cost of maintenance. Consequently we would have nothing left to retire the bonds, and it seems to me these would have to be looked after by making a charge on the grain brought down by this route. That brings one to the statement made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar), that he cannot see how the utilization of the route would enable us to save 10 cents a bushel on the transportation of western grain.
I do not wish to use this sis an argument in support of the Hudson Bay route, but,

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
coming from the West, naturally I am in favour of this route, although probably only as an auxiliary to the St. Lawrence route. I do not think any members from the West have tried to make it appear that the Hudson Bay route would divert traffic which should rightly go down the St. Lawrence. I think the Hudson Bay route would look after a part of the country which at the present time is undeveloped, and even with this route in operation I believe that with the further development of the country which, one might say, is naturally tributary to the St. Lawrence route, a still greater traffic would result from the deepening of this waterway. Therefore the Hudson Bay route does not of necessity enter into this discussion.
It has been well brought out by one hon. gentleman that the activities of combines should be circumscribed to the fullest possible extent, because it appears that the longer our transportation route the more opportunities there are for these combines to get in and steal from the individual who produces the commodity which is being transported. When the confidence of the people is restored by the assurance that combines will not be allowed to intervene between the producer and the ultimate consumer, I think there will not be quite so much apparent opposition to expenditures of this character. And then I do not think parliament will hesitate to grant to the government of the day power to undertake all these projects which have been advocated from time to time.
I only rose to sound a note of warning, for if we take precedent as a guide we are justified in assuming that the cost of deepening the St. Lawrence channel, like every other great undertaking, will exceed the initial estimate by a very large figure indeed, and in this event the benefits which would accrue from
the development and sale of 750,000 horsepower would be more or less neutralized.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to utter a word of protest against what seems to be taken for granted, namely, that the West is opposed to the Welland canal improvement. I am sure that this assumption is not well founded, and can only have arisen because of the fact that operations having been suspended on the Hudson Bay railway, we do not accept the Welland canal as an alternative for the non-completion of the former work. But I am sure that the West is not opposed to the construction of the Welland canal.
Item agreed to.

I assume that everything has been said in connection with the preceding vote, Mr. Chairman. But under the arrangement with the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) we were to discuss under that item the figures which he was to bring down under vote 139 providing for an advance of $73,000,000 to the Canadian National Railway Company. I think my hon. friend has the figures and is ready to table them.
Yes. According to the arrangement, the other day, Mr. Chairman, I was to lay on the table a compilation of comparisons asked for by my hon. friend. I will lay it on the table now.
No. Why not take it as read and incorporate it in Hansard? We want to use it.
I am quite willing to put it in Hansard.

Before this matter goes on, it was pointed out by the leader of the Opposition that there was no notice given that this would be taken up to-day. He tells me that he has an understanding with the government, and I just want to see if I am right, that while the item will be called and the discussion proceeded with, it will not be closed to-night so that he will have an opportunity of preparing whatever may be necessary to be prepared.

What we had in mind was this: This discussion may be a bit lengthy, and we thought we might as well proceed with some of it, but there is no intention of bringing the discussion to a close to-night.
I might say briefly that the report of the Merchant Marine for the year ending December 31, 1922, is in the hands of hon. members. There is nothing much to add to wha* is in that report. It may be asked why the

figures in that report are given for the calendar year instead of for the fiscal year. It is convenient both for the railways and the Merchant Marine that their year should close with the calendar year, so any discrepancy between the figures of the appropriation and the amount given as expended will be accounted for by the fact that the appropriation runs from March 31st to March 31st, while the business year of the Merchant Marine runs from December 31st to December 31st. I do not know that I can add a single figure to what hon. gentlemen have in the report that is before them.

Did I understand the minister to say that this item would not be passed to-night? There are several hon. gentlemen in this section of the House who desire to speak on this vote who are detained at some banquet.

The understanding was that some hon. gentlemen present wished to speak. We are open for speeches, of course. If they take the ground that they do not want either to speak or to put the item through it means a couple of hours wasted.
Usually there is a great rush of hon. members to get on their feet to make a speech, but as no one has risen-
It is a good sign.

-this is an opportunity for me to take up a little time to-night. I rise largely for the purpose of seeking information regarding the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. The other night I used a phrase that perhaps I should not have used when I said that it might be necessary some day to take the ships of the Merchant Marine out into deep water and sink them. I prefaced that remark with something and followed it with something, so I hope it will never be quoted against me. It brought to my mind how dangerous it might be to use phrases of that kind in the House, because I sincerely hope it may never be necessary to do any such thing with the Canadian Merchant Marine.
I have heard a good many things said of the ships of the Canadian Government Merchant	Marine,	but	I	have	neveryet heard	anything	said	in	their	favour,and I would like some information in regard to the building of these ships: who designed them, what trade were they designed for, why is it that when any matter of shipping	comes up	in the House the firstthing you	hear is that	the	ships	of the
Merchant Marine are not suited for that sort of work?

I do not know whether the minister is going to be able to tell us just what sort of trade these ships were built for. I have read some of the past debates in connection with the building of these ships, and I do not intend to enter into that phase of the matter at this time. I realize that they were built at a very expensive time, that a good many of them cost from S160 to $195 per ton, while ships that were built in pre-war times could be built for about $50 per ton, and perhaps they can be built even cheaper to-day. I think a very reasonable thing to do at the outset in connection with the Merchant Marine-I know that this suggestion was made by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) with regard to the government railways, and I think it would be even more applicable to the Merchant Marine-would be to have these ships valued. I am aware that the minister is trying to sell some of them, and it might not be a good thing to value them too low; nevertheless I do not think it will ever be possible for these ships to pay interest and depreciation charges upon their valuation at the time they were built, but if they were valued at what they are actually worth to-day, and some attempt was made to make them pay interest on that amount, there might be reasonable hope that that could be done.
I notice in the report that the deficit after all charges, including depreciation and interest, amounts to $9,649,478.72-a vert large deficit for the people no doubt who pay taxes in this country to make up. I have no doubt that there is going to be a deficit for a long time if an attempt is made to pay interest on the valuation of these ships that were built at such a high cost. I hope we shall get some information during this debate as to what is the matter with the Merchant Marine. Why is it these ships cannot do business on the ocean or on the lakes? We had a discussion the other night about subsidizing a service to the West Indies, and were told that these boats were not suitable for that service. Looking over the debates of past sessions I noticed that the Hon. Mr. Ballantyne made the statement that these ships were suitable for carrying cattle across the Atlantic ocean, but now we are told that they are not suitable for that purpose. The statement was also made in past sessions that the smaller boats of the Merchant Marine were able to compete and would carry grain on the Great Lakes, but now we are told that they cannot compete with the large boats that carry grain that were built especially for that purpose.

I said when I rose to my feet that I rose largely for the purpose of seeking information, because we really ought to know what is the matter. Why is it these boats are unable to compete with other boats? Perhaps I am correct in saying that at the present time there is sufficient shipping in Montreal and other seaports to do all the business that is being offered in the world to-day. I think that is correct. Nevertheless, it seems to me that our boats should be able to take their share of the business. I mentioned the other day that it might be a good idea for the Canadian National Railways to have boats running in connection with the railways that were able to carry cattle across the ocean and set a rate that would be a paying rate. These boats could demonstrate what was a reasonable rate for carrying cattle across the ocean. I have also seen it stated that while these boats are a losing proposition at the present time they bring a certain amount of trade to the Canadian National Railways, and although that results in a deficit so far as the Merchant Marine is concerned it helps to make the railways more paying than they otherwise would be. I believe the time is not far distant, or at all events I look forward to the time when the Canadian National Railways will have a line of ships running in connection with them just as the Canadian Pacific has to-day in connection with their railway. I hope that this Canadian Government Merchant Marine may be only the beginning of a line of ships that will bring trade and create ocean traffic that will help to make our railways pay a great deal better than they are doing to-day.
When I rose I knew that I could throw no light on this matter. I have, to use a nautical expression, been a good deal at sea in regard to these ships, and when I spoke the other day about sinking them in deep water it was only by way of passing a joke. We want to see some value got for these ships, and during this debate I am going to listen in the hope of finding out just what is the trouble, why we have this large deficit, and why we are told continually that these boats are not suitable for this, that and the other trade or any trade we can mention. Immediately we mention the Canadian Government Merchant Marine we are told its vessels are not suited for that kind of work. May I ask, what sort of work they are really suited for?

I do not know whether I will be able to supply the leader of the Progressive party with the information he desires. He is not the only person in Canada who, I

who was Minister of Marine and Fisheries, also made a speech on that occasion, and he told us that they were having two ships built by the Vickers Company at Montreal, one of 8,100 tons dead weight capacity, and another of 4,350 tons. He said that in addition to those vessels another ship of about 5,000 tons was being built by the Wallace Shipbuilding Company, of Vancouver, and another vessel of 3,550 tons by the Collingwood Shipbuilding Company, Collingwood. He said the Dominion government had those four vessels under construction. That was the reason, why, in my opinion, the hon. gentleman who now occupies the distinguished position of Speaker of this House approved of that policy. It was also the reason why the hon. gentleman who was lately Solicitor General in this government also approved of the scheme. Neither of these gentlemen, nor any other member in parliament at that time, thought the government of the day intended to spend $80,000,000 in the construction of these ships. Now, Sir, we have also been told that whilst certain gentlemen were in favour of that scheme, nobody opposed it. But if you will turn to Hansard of 1918 you will find that the then hon. member for Red Deer, Mr. Clark, did oppose the government's shipbuilding programme. He said frankly and freely that he did not believe it was a wise expenditure, or that the policy contemplated was wise. Therefore, while some gentlemen approved of that scheme, other gentlemen in the House at that time did not think it was a wise policy to embark upon even in war time. As far as I am personally concerned I did not object to the expenditure of that money in 1918, principally because I felt that while the war was on and ships were being sunk every day it was a fairly good policy for the government to build ships so long as the war lasted. However, as we all know, the war ceased in November 1918, and at that time the keels of four ships only were laid in the shipyards referred to. I contend, and I have done the same thing for a number of years whenever I spoke on this subject in parliament, that the right and proper thing for the government of the day to have done when the war was over and when every shipyard in Britain, in France, and in the United States was busy building ships, was to have stopped the construction of these vessels. They should have stopped building when ships were partly constructed, and perhaps others were under way, in these shipyards.
My own opinion is that it would have been far better, if this government wanted to
encourage a mercantile marine, to have gone out at that time and endeavoured to make some arrangement with the shipbuilders whereby shipbuilding would have been continued and a Canadian merchant marine, instead of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, would have been built up in this country, as it has been built up in other countries. But instead of that the hon. member who occupied the position of Minister of Marine and Fisheries was determined to go on with his project, and without going into the matter very much further, the result was that $79,000,000 of this country's money was spent in the building of the ships, and these ships, instead of being sold, were operated by what was known a3 the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Limited. My own opinion is that if the government were determined to operate these ships that they never should have put it in this company form, or placed it under the management of a corporation. At the present time there is not one man who is managing these ships, or who is a director of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, who has one dollar invested in the enterprise. I say that is not the right and proper way to run a business, and you can never get satisfaction out of it. It is purely a camouflage that this project which has cost the people of the country $80,000,000 is being run by men who have no financial interest in the matter.
After these ships were completed, in fact before they were all completed, the government commenced operating, and those who are familiar with ship operation will know that, during the first two years these ships were operated, conditions were abnormal in the shipping business, and that, instead of making 10 or 15 per cent on money invested in shipping, as high as 100, 200 and 300 per cent on the cost of ships was made yearly by different firms operating ships in different countries in the world. It would naturally be expected that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine would participate in the business the other people were getting, or in similar business, and would make large profits on the operation of the ships; but if hon. members will look at the statements that have been furnished by the government in connection with this project they will see that, instead of making a fair profit on the ventures, very little money was made in those years when other people were making large sums of money. Now we come to the present day.

Now, if the committee will bear with me, in order that the Progressive leade" and the country may know exactly how I look upon this project and how this project looks to me, I will endeavour in the shortest time possible to give all the information which I have at my command. Jn order to do that it will be necessary for me to go back and review the entire undertaking from the time of its inception. I do not pretend, however, to-night to criticize or condemn Union government or the Conservative government -the Union government for entering into T.he project, or the Conservative government for carrying it out after they came into power in 1921, or after Sir Robert Borden resigned ami the present leader of the Opposition became Prime Minister of Canada. It is useless, in my opinion, for members of parliament, in order to make a point, to go back and throw political mud-shall I call it?-on their opponents and say they were to blame for everything that happened in connectio l with this or that matter. We have arrived with regard to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, at a time when it does not make very much difference whether the Union government are responsible for the building of those ships or not. The question we have to face to-day in this country and in this parliament is, as to whether these ships should continue to be operated or not. If it can be proved conclusively that these vessels are necessary and if-as some people have tried to make out in the past, and are trying to make out now -we must keep them going to help the Canadian National Railways-if that can be proved conclusively then I say this country should carry on the proposition. If, however, it can be shown that these ships are not necessary to carry on the trade of this country, that there are millions of tons of ships on every ocean in the world ready to transport the products of Canada and every other nation, then I say it is not necessary for this government or this country either to keep on paying year after year the deficits on the operation of these ships that we have been paying, or to run government-owned ships in competition with private enterprise.
Now, Sir, as I said, I do not intend to criticize the Union government for the commencement of this project, but in order that the leader of the Progressive party and the House may know exactly what occurred, I should like for a few moments to review exactly what happened in connection with this enterprise in parliament. I think it was in

April, 1918, that Sir Robert Borden, who was then leader of the government, came to this House and proposed that we should vote $25,000,000 for the building of ships in this country. The reason Sir Robert Borden gave at that time for the proposition was, that in view of the fact that hundreds of thousands of tons of shipping were being sunk daily by the German submarines, and in view of the fact that it was necessary in this country to build ships to carry supplies not only to the soldiers at the front but also to the various peoples in Europe, that it would be a good policy on the part of the Canadian people to build ships to help out that very serious situation. Sir Robert Borden, in reviewing the situation at that time, told us that the fourteen shipyards in Canada were busy building ships for the Imperial Munitions Board, which was really a branch of the Imperial government, but he said as soon as these ships were completed it was the intention of the Canadian government to start building ships in those yards with Canadian money and for the Canadian people. We heard it stated in this House a few days ago that not only were the supporters of the Union government favourable to that scheme at that particular time, but that certain hon. gentlemen who were supporters of the Liberal party also favoured it. Indeed it is now said in contradiction, whenever we criticize the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, that members of the Liberal party favoured the scheme. While that is quite true up to a certain degree, yet anybody who takes the trouble to read Hansard of that time will find that when Sir Robert Borden made that proposal there was absolutely no talk of operating ships. Sir Robert Borden only told us that in view of the prevailing conditions Canada was going into the j^hip building business, not into the ship operating business; and any Liberal members who spoke in approval of the scheme at that time never approved of operating the ships which the government intended to build. I do not know that it is necessary to read exactly what Sir Robert Borden then said. I think I have covered the ground very well, but on April 4th, of the same year Mr. Ballantyne, who was the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in the Union government, also spoke in regard to the matter.

Now, Sir, I want to say, first, with regard to these items, that I did not oppose the vote last year of $4,360,720, because in conversation with the then minister he told me-and I quite understood it-that he had not had time to look into the business. The proper thing to have done was to let the bank carry the overdraft, as they were doing, until such time as sufficient ships were sold to pay the deficit. I do not profess to have any legal knowledge; but I noticed the other day that we were discussing all day the question whether it was legal to pay or to lend $2,000,000 to some syndicate to buy or rent a property in Paris. I am not quite clear yet whether we were to buy or to rent this property. I am very doubtful whether this parliament has any legal right to vote to an incorporated company called the Canadian Government Merchant Marine any moneys of this country. This company should stand on its own bottom and pay its deficits out of its assets and not out of money voted by this parliament. As I said, I am not a lawyer, but I am very doubtful if there would be a legal right to pay this. If the money can be paid on a legal technicality, I say that this government had no moral right to pay this large sum of money for that purpose, but the deficit should have been paid out of the assets of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.

In view of these facts, as I said a moment ago, is it wise for us to continue making up these deficits year after year? Are these ships necessary to do the country's business? I claim they are not necessary, and in this opinion I am upheld by a number of eminent authorities in various parts of the Dominion. For instance, the Ottawa Journal, in an editorial which appeared shortly after this annual statement was issued by the Canadian Government Merchant Marnie, said:
The worst feature of the whole proposition is that this loss is sustained without any visible advantage. True, the statement shows that the vessels turned over certain freight and passengers to the Canadian National Railways but the figures cannot be considered as even the shadow of justification for a nine million dollar deficit. Moreover, the corporation operating the ships apparently made them part of an Atlantic combine for the heightening of freights; this, at a time when there was a surplus of shipping, making them of no value whatever to the Canadian exporter.
In addition to this criticism, the Montreal Gazette-which perhaps is one of the sanest papers in Canada-has published several editorials severely condemning the slowness of this government and its predecessors for allowing these vessels to be operated any longer, and in every one it has shown conclusively that their continued operation is not necessary in the interests of the country. Then another paper, the Journal of Commerce, had this to say:
Canada's state-owned merchant marine, according to reports published by the Department of Commerce, returned1 a deficit of over $9,000,000 on a gross income of a little better than $10,700,000 during 1921. According to the best information available this condition was not improved during the calendar year 1922. The latest complete financial statement available (1921) illustrates the possibilities of government ownership of merchant vessels.
It has been argued by the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) and one or two other hon. gentlemen that these ships were in a combine with a New York Canadian National Railways. I do not think that any shipping man will agree with such
[Mr. Duff.)
a statement, because if the Canadian National Railways have efficient freight agents there is absolutely no reason why they cannot arrange with shipping companies to take freight at the seaboard for transportation overseas at a cheaper rate than it is costing us to-day by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. After all, what percentage of the goods handled by the Canadian National Railways to Vancouver, Montreal, Quebec, Halifax, St. John or Portland, was taken overseas by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine? If hon. gentlemen will look up Hansard of April 7th, 1921, they will find that statement in the speech which I then made. We find that somebody in an endeavour to promote business for the government boats entered into an arrangement with certain New York shipping interests

to come into what is known as the New York Shipping Pool. Now a gentleman who does not know anything about shipping, and who goes to New York among the shipping sharks to enter into an arrangement with them, well, all I can say is Heaven help him. Does my hon. friend think that the Combines Bill of the present government will have any effect on this combine?

I have not read it yet, and I do not know what it contains, but evidently the government has not done much so far to get the Merchant Marine out of the New York combine. Our steamers are still in this combine. That was admitted by the gentleman who is at the head of the freight department of'the Merchant Marine. He said that they still sat in when these rates were fixed. I want to say that is a pretty poor excuse for the freight manager of the Merchant Marine to give to the people of this country, that these ships were not in the combine and that all he did was to sit in when the agents of the other lines were discussing rates. I say that no business men in this country would allow any other man who was not in agreement with them to come into their office to a directors' meeting and listen to all that was going on unless they knew he was in hearty agreement with what was proposed at that meeting. So I say the Merchant Marine were in the pool, and I think it is likely they are still in that New York ring.
They were not according to the last account.
That is because your committee frightened them.
Does the hon. member think it is necessary that that condition should continue now that we know the facts?

I say that in spite of the fact that the Canadian Merchant Marine were keeping up the rates to the same figure as the other lines they had a deficit in two years of 318,000,000, and does my hon. friend want to argue that we should have their rates reduced and bring about a deficit of say $25,000,000? I do not think he wants that.
They may get more business in that case.

They cannot get more business because the other ships can get business ahead of them every time. All the Merchant Marine ships get is what is left and the little that the Canadian National Railways put their way. Just look over the ships of the Merchant Marine in the different ports. While they have cargoes when they leave this country, and most of them are cargoes of lumber which any old windjammer can carry, coming back they have practically no cargo at all.
Why do they not get cargoes? Is it due to mismanagement or to the class of vessels?

I do not think it is mismanagement at all. I think the gentleman in charge of the Merchant Marine had a pretty hard row to hoe. The government should never have thrown these sixty-three ships at him. No other shipping company in the world ever bought sixty-three ships inside of twelve months. They buy one, two, three or four ships and gradually build up their holdings. Consequently I say the gentleman in charge had a pretty hard row to hoe, and he has done remarkably well under the circumstances. There are other causes why these ships do not pay and one is that they are suitable only for carrying bulk cargoes. They can take lumber but everybody knows that for the last two years there has been no money in that. Here is my idea of how to do that: This subsidy has been paid for a number of years either to the Royal Mail Packet Company or to some other company. At the time this subsidy was paid freight rates were much lower than they are at the present time, and there was not as much freight offering for West India ports, with the result that, perhaps, it was necessary for previous governments, whether it was a Liberal government or a Conservative government, in order to keep up the traffic between the West India Islands to give a subsidy to a' line of steamships. But during the war years when the Royal Mail Packet Company was running on this route the business and the rates of freight were sufficient and they did not require a subsidy. That is the reason why I opposed the subsidy of $388,000 to the Royal Mail Packet Company in 1919. But what has happened since? Here is what the late government did and what the present government are now doing. Both governments are eqully to blame in my opinion and here is what they did. When the war was over, I think it was in 1919, the Canadian Government Merchant Marine management deliberately put four steamships, if I remember correctly, on the same route or practically the same route over which the Royal Mail Packet Company plies. The result was that immediately both these lines of ships were dividing the freight that was offering. Consequently there was not enough cargo offering for both ships to be filled. Both lines of ships were carrying half cargoes and their holds were half empty. Sometimes on the return trip the vessels of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine hardly had enough molasses for the crew to eat on the way home and the ships of the Royal Mail Packet Company were almost as bad.

molasses to mix with their rum. After that when it was found that the Royal Mail Packet Company were losing business due to the fact that there was a competing line of government ships, or practically government ships, the manager of the former company came to Ottawa. The statement of 1919 shows a profit of $1,400,000; the 1920 statement shows a profit of $600,000; that is $2,000,000 altogether. The $500,000 was paid out of this $2,000,000 and after allowing for depreciation left a surplus of $1,000,000, the amount my hon. friend stated. The $500,000 was deducted a year before the $1,000,000 surplus was shown. What good is it for the minister to argue that the $500,000 came out of the $1,000,000 surplus? It came out of the $2,000,000 profits that the company was supposed to earn.
We will have a statement made up to date to-morrow concerning all the transactions.

The hon. member for Lunenburg asked a rhetorical question as to what Sir Henry Thornton would know about boats. Well, to be fair to Sir Henry Thornton I should think he operated in England just about as many miles of ocean traffic as he did land traffic. Certainly for fifty .per cent of his total mileage he would have water mileage to the same extent.
That is coastal boats and passenger boats.
No, boats to the Continent and back, to Flushing and other points. I think Sir Henry Thornton has had a good deal of experience in regard to boats.
What was the extreme distance between the termini of the route of these ships?

If we were to follow up that question it would lead to other considerations concerning Sir Henry Thornton and I do not care to follow the subject. Certainly there is just as big a difference between the termini in this country, from the Pacific on the one side and the Atlantic on the other as there is on these water routes in connection with the railways in England. But I do not think that is a fair way of looking at it. I just wanted to point out that he knew something about this marine business.
I should say for the benefit of the leader of the Opposition who asked as to the cost, that the cost of construction was greater than he thinks. The original cost was $191.95 per ton on the average. With that can be compared the cost of the American Shipping Board for the work done at the same time, which was $215 per ton. Our work actually was $23.05 a ton cheaper than was the work done in the yards that are nearest to us and where the fairest comparison can be made. I wanted to ask a further question, and that is, is it true that the business of the Canadian National Railways is carried on in so far as
Supply-Merchant Marine

lake and water services are concerned at a charge 100 per cent greater than there is any justification for? The minister shakes his head. I think that was a very serious charge made by the hon. member for Lunenburg. If it be true that the practice of the railway is to subsidize these boats by paying them twice as much for their services as would be paid to other boats, it is rather an extraordinary situation. The hon. member has given the exact figures here to-night. It may be that he is entirely mistaken in his information, but I think the minister should go into that and let us have some information on that point. On the other hand, to be fair, Sir Henry Thornton, who knows about shipping because he has done almost as much shipping work in England as railway work, says that these boats have been a great feeder to his system. I would like to know what the minister thinks of that.

If hon. gentlemen will permit me, as we do not intend to pass this vote to-night I would like the item to stand. With regard to the figures given by the hon. member for Lunenburg I think if the hon. member looks at his figures as to charges made by these boats of the Merchant Marine he will find that he has made a mistake. This is my information. However, that can be looked into.
Would the committee allow me to put through item 358 for the running of the canals all over Canada? This item is some $33,000 less than last year. It is for the purpose of the working of our canals.

Before we leave the Merchant Marine, some time ago I asked a question of the ex-Minister of Finance in regard to shipping and he told me that he wanted to finish his sentence. He was a long time finishing it.
Speaking of shipping, I represent a county that built the largest sailing ships that were ever built in Canada. The W. D. Lawrence was built at Maitland in the county of Hants. I did not rise for the purpose of prolonging this discussion. I heard some very pertinent questions put to the minister and the hon. member for Lunenburg by the leader of the Progressive party, and I did not hear him get many, answers. I simply want to say that I absolutely agree with the hon. member for Lunenburg in the criticism which he has made of the Merchant Marine. The time has come in this country when the Merchant Marine should be disposed of. I believe that we are running riot as regards government ownership of all sorts nf things. My hon.
Jfcir Henrv Drayton.]
friend from Toronto in the course of his address asked if these ships were thoroughly equipped in every manner for the purpose of carrying on business. Now, any person who knows anything about ships or who has ever lived near the sea shore and has seen some of the ships of the Merchant Marine knows that they are absolutely unfit for ninety per cent of the trade which offers to-day. Any person who goes aboard them knows that the hatches are so situated that it is absolutely impossible to load or unload with quick despatch. Nor as my hon. friend from Lunenburg says, are they fit for the transportation of cattle. It is true they may be able to take over a few cattle, but they cannot take them over with profit to this country. I think the quicker we get clear of these boats the better. If we are going to have a shipping trade at all, let us get ships that are able to take the trade offering to the Old Country, ships of the proper type, not the ships of the Merchant Marine built not for the purposes of trade but for the purpose of supplying employment to people during the war and giving contracts to friends of the late government. The quicker we get rid of them the better it will be in the interests of Canadian industry.
I would suggest with all due deference to the Minister of Railways, who is an excellent man, that the quicker the administration of shipping in this country is put in the hands of men who are seamen-and if he wants me to find him seamen and will give me the patronage I will bring them up even from that historic county of Hants-the better it will be, but so long as the shipping interests of this country and its ships are to be run by a bunch of landlubbers so long will the people of Canada be compelled to pay an immense amount in deficits. It is not fair to the people of this Dominion that we should go on year after year voting money to pay deficits on these ships. It is all very well to vote the money. Then during the recess Governor General's warrants will be issued for the purpose of supplying money to a lot of landlubbers to carry on the foolish scheme, and if I or any other hon. member goes to the minister and asks for something in the way of improvement of port facilities or improvement in the trade facilities in his constituency he is told that he cannot get it because the Finance Minister has not got the money for it and could not make that particular grant. But in the meantime we are voting millions of money to the Canadian National Railways -and the quicker we get rid of that the better, though that opinion may not be received with joy by most people in the country but

Vimy Ridge
we have them upon us and we have to take care of them-and millions more for the Merchant Marine. Let us get rid of these ships of the Merchant Marine, this great octopus. If we cannot do anything better with it than we have done in the past I would ask that it be given to some son of Israel to be put on the dump pile. It is not fair to the people of this Dominion to go on voting money to make up deficits on the Merchant Marine year after year. I was hoping the hon. member for Lunenburg would move for the cutting out of the vote. Liberal as I am, I would vote against any government that persisted in continuing votes for the Canadian Merchant Marine.

I was not intending to speak on this question but when we have such great authorities as we have heard tonight differing so much about the utility of these boats it seems to me the only way to settle it is to give them a better trial than they have got yet. I have listened to the exMinister of Finance and he tells me that these vessels are of modern pattern and built like freighters, and are as good as could be put into the service. I want to believe that story because we are in need of boats. On the other hand the hon. member for Lunenburg and the hon. member for Hants tell us almost that they are not worth the powder to blow them up. Now which is true? I do not know. Coming from the West, as my hon. friend says, I am supposed to be classified among the landlubbers. Well I do not object to being that at all but I tell you what I want: I want to get some of these boats that will carry cattle overseas. We have been in correspondence with Sir Henry Thornton and he has finally decided to try out six of these boats for this purpose, and before they are blown to Kingdom come I want to give them a trial. We have been discussing this thing three or four times this winter and spring. Now we have got to it again and fitting them up temporarily it is probable that without very much expenditure they will probably be ready in ten days or so. After a trial we will know more about them. They will have served their purpose, for three months they will have had a fair trial and then we shall know definitely one way or the other. We shall probably then have some information as to what disposition ought to be made of these particular vessels, or some larger ones that may be put into service for this special purpose we have in view.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

subsubtopic: THANKS OF FRENCH PRESIDENT FOR JOINT RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that I have received the following letter:
Ottawa, 12th June, 1923.
Sir,-I have it in command from His Excellency the Governor General to transmit to you copy of a despatch from the Secretary of State for the Colonies enclosing copy of a note from the French Ministry for Foreign Affairs, conveying the thanks of the President of the Republic for the joint resolution of the Canadian Houses of Parliament regarding the gift of land on Vimy Ridge by the French government.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Signed) Joseph Pope. Under-Secretary of State for
External Affairs.
The Hon. Speaker of the House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Downing Street, 29 May, 1923. My Lord,-With reference to my despatch No. 193 of the 28th of April, I have the honour to transmit to Your Excellency, to be laid before your ministers, the accompanying copy of a note from the French Ministry for Foreign Affairs, conveying the thanks of the president of the Republic for the joint resolution of the Canadian Houses of parliament regarding the gift of land on Vimy Ridge by the French government.
I have the honour to be, My Lord,
Your Lordship's most obedient humble servant.
(Signed) Devonshire.
His Excellency,
The Right Honourable Lord Byng op Vimy, G.C.B., G.C.M.G.,
M.V.O., etc., etc., etc.
(Translation)
French Republic Ministry of Foreign Affairs
America.
Monsieur l'Ambassadeur.
I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of the letter dated the 28th April last, and in which Mr. Erio Phipps was kind enough to enclose two copies of a resolution adopted by the Canadian parliament, to accept the gift by France of a parcel of land, on Vimy ridge, where it is proposed to erect a monument recalling the achievements of the Canadian soldiers.
Monsieur le President of the Republic, to whom these documents were presented in pursuance of the wish of the Canadian government, requests me to convey his thanks and wishes you to transmit to the government of Canada the expression of his gratitude.
Mr. Millerand has appreciated most highly the so cordial terms which the Canadian parliament made use of to express its gratefulness to the French government.
Kindly accept, Sir, the assurances of my highest esteem.
(Signed) Poincare.
Paris, May 15, 1923.
On motion of Mr. Fielding the House adjourned at 12.20 a.m. (Wednesday).
